canonical_topic: NGL liquefaction, storage, transport, and sourcing
definition: Heavier NGLs such as propane and butane liquefy easily under only moderate compression, shrinking roughly 270-fold in volume, which lets them be stored and moved as liquids and released as gas on demand; they are recovered from raw natural gas at processing plants or from crude oil at refineries.
core_idea: NGLs' ability to liquefy under modest pressure makes them practical to store, ship, and dispense (e.g., a grill propane tank), and they are commonly recovered as a byproduct of natural gas processing and oil refining, especially from shale plays developed via fracking.
key_points: Compression liquefies NGLs like propane and butane far more easily than methane.
Liquefied NGLs occupy roughly 1/270th the volume of the gaseous form.
Only moderate pressure is needed for this compression, enabling practical liquid storage and transport.
A common consumer use is grill/cooking fuel: propane is stored liquefied under pressure and evaporates to gas when a valve is opened.
NGLs are commonly dissolved within crude oil or natural gas and are abundant in shale deposits accessed via fracking.
NGLs are separated out at natural gas processing plants (from gas) or at refineries (from crude oil).
relationships: Cheap fracked natural gas undercut U.S. carbon legislation
